title: How to Fight Fair
excerpt: The goal of a marital argument is not to win. A marriage where someone keeps winning is a marriage where someone keeps losing.
body:
The first lie about conflict in marriage is that good marriages do not have much of it. The couples who never fight are usually the ones where someone has gone underground, where the peace is being bought by one person swallowing themselves whole, and that bill always comes due with interest. Conflict is not the enemy of a marriage. Contempt is. Learning the difference may be the most practical skill a married person can develop.

You married a separate human being with a separate history and a separate set of wounds and a separate way of loading the dishwasher that is, you will discover, somehow morally wrong. You are going to fight. The question is never whether. The question is what the fight is for, and whether anyone walks out of it bleeding.

## Win the marriage, not the argument

The goal of a marital argument is not to win. I know the rush of landing the unanswerable point, the line your spouse cannot rebut, and I know how I feel an hour later, because I understand what I actually did. A marriage where someone keeps winning is a marriage where someone keeps losing, and you cannot build a covenant on a standing score. Every time you win the argument you lose a little of the marriage, until one day the losses add up to something you cannot pay.

The goal is to understand and be understood and to come out the other side still on the same team. Everything else is technique in service of that, or it is poison dressed up as technique.

## Fight the real thing

There is a difference between the thing you are fighting about and the thing you are fighting for. The thing you are fighting about is the credit card statement, the in-laws, the unmade plan. The thing you are fighting for is almost always one of a few deep things: to feel respected, to feel chosen, to feel that you are not carrying this alone, to feel safe. The surface fights are endless reruns of the same three or four underlying ones. Ask yourself, in the middle of it, what am I actually fighting for here, and you will sometimes find the statement was never the issue.

## The moves that turn a fight into a wound

Four behaviors corrode a marriage, and researchers who have watched thousands of couples confirm what Scripture always said about the corrosive tongue. I have watched all four nearly do damage in my own house.

Contempt is the worst. Anger says you hurt me. Contempt says you are beneath me. It comes out in the eye roll, the mocking tone, the of course you would. It does not attack a behavior, it attacks a person, and a person can only answer an attack on their worth by attacking back or going cold. Keep contempt out of your mouth. Your spouse's dignity stays off the table no matter how hot it gets.

The kitchen sink is the second, where the fight about tonight becomes the fight about everything and you reach back three years to haul up old grievances. Fight the thing in front of you. One issue. If the old things keep surfacing, that means they were buried, not resolved, but the middle of a new fight is not the place to exhume them.

The universal quantifier is the third. You always, you never. These are almost always false and your spouse knows it, so you hand them an easy out: they argue about the word always instead of the actual hurt. Drop it. Say what happened this time.

Stonewalling is the fourth and the sneakiest, because it does not look like aggression. Going silent. Walking out. Shutting the face into a wall. It feels like self-control to the one doing it and like abandonment to the one left behind. Sometimes you genuinely need to stop because you are flooded. Fine. But say it. I am too far gone to do this well right now, I am not leaving you, I need twenty minutes, and I will come back. The difference between a wise pause and a punishing silence is whether you promised to come back.

## Anger is not the sin

The church often shames anger and is frequently wrong to. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes, which means the anger and the sin are separable. The issue is never that you feel it hot. The issue is what the heat does. Heat that burns the issue is fine. Heat that burns the person is not. If your volume makes your spouse go silent and small, then whatever it feels like from inside, from the outside it is working as a weapon, and love requires you to care more about the wound than the catharsis.

And to the one who avoids: peacekeeping is not peacemaking. The peacekeeper avoids the conflict to keep the surface calm. The peacemaker enters it to make a deeper peace on the other side. Jesus blessed the second one. If you keep the peace by never saying the hard thing, you are not protecting the marriage. You are starving it and calling the starvation kindness.

## The repair is what saves you

No couple fights perfectly. The healthy ones are not the ones who never cross the line. They are the ones who notice and come back. The repair can be small: a hand on the shoulder, a softer voice, I am sorry, that was beneath me, can we start over. Whether the repair gets received matters more than how bad the fight got. A marriage is not measured by the absence of rupture. It is measured by the speed of repair.

## This week

Next time you feel the fight starting, do one thing: before you respond, ask yourself what you are actually fighting for, and name that instead of the surface complaint. I am not angry about the dishes, I am feeling like I carry this house alone. Say the real thing. And if you cross a line, do not wait for a clean moment to repair. Repair badly and fast. The marriages that last are not the ones without wounds. They are the ones that learned to heal faster than they hurt.
